turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.

I'm sitting down. I have a client call at 4:40, so I have about twenty minutes. Owen found out about a zero from the gradebook, on his phone, in the middle of class. Why didn't anyone call me first, Hale?
I did. I entered the zero on November 3rd without calling you, and our procedure says I should have called first. I'm sorry Owen found out on his phone in class. That's my mistake, not his.
Okay. Then you know the procedure says you call before any mark goes in. So what is the zero based on, Hale? Show me.

This is the document's version history from Google Docs, printed. You can open it from Owen's account tonight and see the same thing. Created Wednesday, October 28 at 11:31 PM with only a title. At 11:52 PM, 612 words arrive in one edit. At 11:58, another 794 in one edit. After that, 23 minutes of small changes, font, his name, spacing. Nothing before Wednesday night.
Turn it toward me. Okay. Read me the first edit again, the 612 words, and the time.
The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: 'The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile.' That line isn't in Hamlet. Search any edition online tonight and you won't find it.
"Not in Hamlet." Okay. Put that in writing, with the edition you checked and the line number. And the version history, where I can see it tonight. What exactly are you asking Owen to accept?

The first edit was 612 words at 11:52 PM. I'll put the quote in writing with the Folger edition. Third thing: on October 15th Owen handed in an outline arguing Hamlet delays out of cowardice. Here it is, with his name and the date. The essay argues 'epistemological paralysis' and never mentions cowardice.

Okay. October 15th, the outline, cowardice. Now the essay says "epistemological paralysis" and drops it. That's a change in argument, Hale, and I want to hear you say whether you're claiming he didn't write the second version.

On November 2nd, after class, I asked him about the essay for five minutes and wrote notes the same day. I asked what 'epistemological paralysis' means. He said 'like, being stuck'. He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about.
"Like, being stuck." Okay. A five-minute chat after class, with notes. Is that the whole basis, or is there more?

There's more. His in-class writing from September 24th: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited to act, scene and line. Both are in his file; you can request copies.
Okay. September 24th, forty minutes, 380 words, comma splices. Now the essay has no comma splices and nine quotations. You're telling me his writing improved in six weeks. Is that your claim, Hale?
And yes, the school's AI checker said 94 percent. I know those tools are unreliable, and I'm not resting on it.

"Not resting on it." Good. Then the score doesn't count for much in this room. Now, on the nine quotations and the in-class sample: do you have the sample itself, the 380 words, or only your summary of it?

I have the sample itself, here, his handwriting. Here's what I'm proposing. I'm not asking you or Owen to admit anything. Our procedure allows a supervised rewrite for a first concern. He writes it with me, in a room, on his own. If it holds up, the new mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record.

Okay. A supervised rewrite, in a room, with you. Now I want the rest of it in writing before anyone signs: private, not in front of his class, and "nothing goes on file" in the terms themselves. Can you put that in an email tonight?
I'd also take the zero off the gradebook view until the rewrite is marked, so he isn't looking at it every day.

Okay. Take it off the gradebook view today, and say so in the email. Then the rewrite, private, nothing on file, all in writing. Put it in an email tonight, and I'll have my answer by tomorrow morning. Thursday, November 12, at nine. Is that workable for you?
Thursday at nine works. I'll email tonight: zero off the gradebook view today, supervised rewrite, private, not in front of the class, nothing on file if it holds up.
Okay. Send it tonight, copy the principal, and I'll read it before nine. If anything about the rewrite is not in the email, I won't agree to it.
Can I ask you one thing, off the record? We've got a parent night in two weeks and other families are going to be in your spot. What should they know walking in?
"Off the record" is still this room, Hale. Owen. Nine o'clock Thursday, in writing, with "nothing on file" in it.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
To: Hale
Cc: Principal's office
Subject: Owen Kalinowski, English 30-1 essay, November 10 meeting

Hale,

Following our meeting today, here are my terms as I understand them. Please reply in writing by 9:00 AM Thursday, November 12 to confirm or correct them.

The zero is removed from the gradebook view today.
Owen completes a supervised rewrite of the essay, in a private room, with you present, and not in front of his class.
If the rewrite demonstrates the learning, its mark replaces the original and nothing is placed on his record.

Until I see those terms confirmed in writing, I am not agreeing to anything else.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: fallback position, with a conditional agreement to a last-position supervised rewrite that is not yet confirmed in writing.
Moved at: "I have the sample itself, here, his handwriting."
Slipped at: "Off the record, what should they know walking in?"
